To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

long-term low-doses of mixtures of environmental oestrogens are capable of increasing the proliferation of breast cells, and that these proliferative effects may be enhanced by the simultaneous presence of oestradiol.
long-term low-doses of environmental oestrogens can act synergistically to increase breast cancer risk.

“Exposure to environmental oestrogens in low doses over a lifetime is a significant factor in the development of breast cancers.” This is a significant finding because it suggests a possible mechanism by which the incidence of breast cancer is increasing in the absence of a change in genetic factors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the long-term low-doses of environmental oestrogens, and how these might act in concert with endogenous hormones to increase the risk of breast cancer.
the long-term effects of low-dose exposure of breast tissue to environmental chemicals capable of mimicing or interfering with oestradiol action.
the potential effects of long-term low dose exposures to complex mixtures of chemicals which mimic the action of oestrogen.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

no clear association has yet been made between exposure to any single environmental chemical or to mixtures of chemicals and the development of human breast cancer,7–16 but the possibility of a long-term low-does effect of complex mixtures on breast cancer risk remains.
the association between breast cancer and environmental chemicals remains unclear and that the evidence is not sufficient to support or refute a link.
there is no clear evidence that environmental oestrogens are associated with increased risk of breast cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that the oestrogenicity of environmental mixtures of chemicals is greater than the additive effect of the sum of their individual oestrogenicities and that this effect is dependent on the dose of the mixture.
the effects of environmental chemicals on breast tissue may be more complex than previously thought.

the effects of low-dose exposure of the human mammary gland to environmental oestrogen mimics are not simply additive but are complex, with a range of interactions that are both synergistic and antagonistic.17,18
Environmental oestrogins and the mammary gland: the importance of timing
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of environmental oestrogens on breast cancer risk should be assessed not only by the presence or absence of individual chemicals but by the total oestrogenic activity of the mixture.
it is not just the amount of a particular chemical that matters, but the total amount of all chemicals that have the potential to mimic oestrogen.
we should not be looking for one or even a few chemicals as the cause of breast cancer.
